A visual guide to model diagnostics

The life of residuals

Every regression model leaves something behind. The fitted line gets all the attention, but the part of the data it fails to explain (the residuals) quietly holds the best evidence about whether the model can be trusted.

If you've ever run plot() on a regression in R and squinted at the four panels it gives you, this is for you. It's the story of those leftovers: where they come from, how we line them up, and what they have to say.

Scroll to begin ↓

Meet our data: 40 penguins from the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. For each bird we know two things: its body mass in grams, and the length of its bill in millimeters.

Plot one against the other and a pattern jumps out: heavier penguins tend to have longer bills.

But the relationship isn't perfect. Penguins with the same weight can still have quite different bills.

A linear regression sums up the trend with one line, the line that fits the points best:

Each extra 100 g of penguin comes with about half a millimeter more bill. Mass explains about 78% of the variation in bill length ().

But look closely: no penguin sits exactly on the line. The vertical gap between what we observed and what the model predicted is the residual:

Green penguins have longer bills than the model predicted; red ones have shorter bills.

Each residual is just a number, measured in millimeters. The biggest miss is a 3,725 g penguin whose bill is 4.61 mm shorter than predicted.

Least squares picks the line that makes the squared residuals add up to as little as possible. One result: the residuals always add up to zero.

To study the residuals by themselves, we strip away everything else. First we flatten the line, taking each penguin's gap along with it.

Then we let go of body mass. Each residual slides to its own value on a single number line. Negative on the left, positive on the right, and the balance point is exactly zero.

Millimeters only make sense for this model. To make residuals comparable, we divide each one by their standard deviation ().1

Notice that the dots don't move. Only the ruler changes. The residuals are now in units of "standard deviations from zero."

Now let them fall. Stacking the residuals into bins half a standard deviation wide turns the number line into a histogram.

Every block is still one penguin.

This shape matters. The p-values and confidence intervals from a regression assume the residuals are roughly normally distributed.

The blue curve smooths our pile into a shape. The black curve is the benchmark: what 40 draws from a perfect bell curve would look like.

They aren't identical, with a bump here and a gap there, but that's normal for a small sample.

Histograms change with the bin sizes you choose, so statisticians use a sharper tool: the quantile–quantile (Q–Q) plot.

To see how it works, picture each distribution as a vase. Our pile of residuals and its blue curve tip onto their side to make one vase. The black bell curve drops below to make the other. The shapes differ, but both vases hold exactly the same amount of water.

Keep scrolling to pour water into both vases at the same rate, starting from the low end.

At every moment, each water line marks a quantile: the value that this share of the distribution falls below. Plot one water line against the other and you trace out the Q–Q plot.

Each time another 1/40 of the water goes in, the water line reaches the next residual, and it leaves the vase for its spot on the plot.2

If both vases had the same shape, every dot would land on the diagonal. Where our vase is narrower, the dots climb more steeply; where it's wider, they level off.

Ours hug the diagonal, so the residuals are close enough to normal.

The Q–Q plot showed our residuals have the right overall shape. Now we check they keep that shape everywhere.

For that we use a residuals vs. fitted plot: each residual lines up with its penguin's predicted bill length. The shaded band is where most misses should land.

If the model works equally well everywhere, the dots stay in the band from left to right. Ours do, with just one slightly outside.

That's the whole life of a residual, told in the three diagnostic plots:

  • Histogram: the overall shape at a glance. Good for spotting skew or a second bump.
  • Q–Q plot: a point-by-point check against the bell curve. Good for tails and outliers.
  • Residuals vs. fitted: the misses across the model's predictions. Good for curves and funnels.

For our penguins, all three look healthy. The line can be trusted.

Notes

  1. To keep the dots still, this story standardizes by dividing every residual by the same number, their standard deviation. R's plot() uses rstandard() instead, which also accounts for each point's leverage: . For these penguins the two versions never differ by more than 0.06 SD.
  2. The residuals' vase is drawn as a smooth curve, but its water line follows the actual sorted residuals, so the Q–Q trace passes exactly through every dot. As a result, the water in that vase only approximately matches the share poured.

Data: palmerpenguins (Horst, Hill & Gorman), a sample of 40 Adélie and Gentoo penguins. Artwork by Allison Horst. The Q–Q vases follow Stine (2016). Built with d3. Set in Open Sans and Chillax by Indian Type Foundry.
